question: Which of the following is NOT one of the CPU scheduling criteria?
hint: The criteria are measured in time or in processes completed.
explanation: Slide 5.8: the scheduling criteria are CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time and response time.

question: The recent trend of placing multiple processor cores on the same physical chip produces:
hint: The result is faster and consumes less power.
explanation: Slide 5.33: the recent trend is to place multiple processor cores on the same physical chip (multicore processors), which is faster and consumes less power.

question: Gradually increasing the priority of processes that have been waiting in the system for a long time is called:
hint: It is the solution, not the problem.
explanation: Slide 5.19: problem - starvation (low-priority processes may never execute); solution - aging (as time progresses, increase the priority of the process).

question: When low-priority processes may wait for a very long time or never get to execute, the problem is called:
hint: Other processes keep getting ahead of them.
explanation: Slide 5.19: starvation - low-priority processes may never execute.

question: Scheduling-algorithm optimization criteria include all of the following EXCEPT:
hint: Time spent by processes should go down, not up.
explanation: Slide 5.9: max CPU utilization, max throughput, min turnaround time, min waiting time, min response time.

question: When comparing two CPU scheduling algorithms, the better one (other things equal) has:
hint: Throughput counts completed processes per time unit.
explanation: Slide 5.9: the optimization goal is maximum throughput, so the algorithm with higher throughput is considered better.

question: CPU scheduling aims to:
options: Maximize CPU utilization and minimize response time
Minimize CPU utilization and maximize response time
Keep the CPU idle as much as possible
hint: Keep the CPU as busy as possible.
explanation: Slides 5.8-5.9: CPU utilization should be maximized (keep the CPU as busy as possible) and response time minimized.

question: Which scheduling algorithm is optimal, giving the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes?
hint: Its difficulty is knowing the length of the next CPU request.
explanation: Slide 5.12: SJF is optimal - it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.

question: Which module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
hint: The scheduler chooses; this module hands over the CPU.
explanation: Slide 5.7: the dispatcher module gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.

question: In which scheduling algorithm can the convoy effect happen?
hint: Short processes get stuck behind a long one that arrived earlier.
explanation: Slide 5.11: FCFS suffers from the convoy effect - a short process behind a long process.

question: The convoy effect is:
options: Short processes waiting behind a long process
Increasing the priority of old processes
The time to stop one process and start another
hint: Think of slow traffic behind a truck.
explanation: Slide 5.11: convoy effect - short process behind long process.

question: Consider one CPU-bound process and many I/O-bound processes under FCFS. Which processes suffer from the convoy effect?
options: The short I/O-bound processes stuck behind the long CPU-bound process
The CPU-bound process stuck behind the I/O-bound ones
No process, since FCFS has no convoy effect
hint: Who has the long CPU burst?
explanation: Slide 5.11: the convoy effect is short processes waiting behind a long process; with one CPU-bound and many I/O-bound processes, the I/O-bound ones wait behind the CPU-bound one.

question: Another name for the short-term scheduler is the:
hint: It selects a process from the ready queue and allocates it a CPU core.
explanation: Slides 5.6-5.7: the CPU scheduler (short-term scheduler) selects from among the processes in the ready queue and allocates a CPU core to one of them.

question: When the time quantum is very large, Round Robin behaves like:
hint: Every process finishes within its first time slice.
explanation: Slide 5.15: performance - q large => FIFO (FCFS).

question: SJF and priority scheduling suffer from the __________ problem, which can be solved by __________.
hint: Low-priority (or long) processes might never run.
explanation: Slide 5.19: SJF is a priority scheduling algorithm; the problem is starvation and the solution is aging.

question: Which CPU-scheduling algorithm is always preemptive?
hint: Its preemption is driven by a timer interrupt every quantum.
explanation: Slide 5.15: in RR, after the time quantum elapses the process is preempted and added to the end of the ready queue. SJF and priority can be preemptive or not; FCFS is nonpreemptive.

question: SJF is a special case of priority scheduling where the priority is:
options: The inverse of the predicted next CPU burst time
hint: Shorter jobs get better priority.
explanation: Slide 5.19: SJF is priority scheduling where priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst time.

question: Dispatch latency is:
options: The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running
The time a process spends in the ready queue
The time from submission to completion
The length of a time quantum
hint: It is the cost of handing the CPU over.
explanation: Slide 5.7: dispatch latency - time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running.

question: In Round Robin scheduling, as the time quantum increases, the average turnaround time:
options: Varies (it does not change in one fixed direction)
hint: Look at the graph of turnaround time versus time quantum.
explanation: Slide 5.18: 'Turnaround Time Varies With The Time Quantum' - the graph is not monotonic.

question: Which of the following scheduling algorithms must be nonpreemptive?
hint: Two of the others have both preemptive and nonpreemptive versions.
explanation: Slides 5.10, 5.14 and 5.19: SJF has a preemptive version (SRTF), priority can be preemptive or nonpreemptive, RR is preemptive; FCFS runs each process until it finishes or waits.

question: The strategy of allowing a process that is logically runnable to be temporarily suspended (the CPU is taken away from it) is called:
hint: The process did not ask to give up the CPU.
explanation: Slide 5.6: scheduling when a process switches from running to ready (or waiting to ready) is preemptive; the running process loses the CPU even though it could continue.

question: Which scheduling algorithm allocates the CPU first to the process that requests the CPU first?
hint: It is also the simplest algorithm.
explanation: Slide 5.10: FCFS allocates the CPU in order of arrival.

question: The SJF algorithm executes first the process:
options: With the shortest next CPU burst
hint: Each process is associated with the length of its next CPU burst.
explanation: Slide 5.12: SJF associates each process with the length of its next CPU burst and schedules the process with the shortest time.

question: CPU scheduling becomes more complex when:
hint: The slide title is Multiple-Processor Scheduling.
explanation: Slide 5.31: CPU scheduling is more complex when multiple CPUs are available.

question: Scheduling is nonpreemptive only when it takes place because a process:
options: Switches from running to waiting, or terminates
Switches from running to ready, or from waiting to ready
hint: In these cases the process gives up the CPU by itself.
explanation: Slide 5.6: scheduling decisions happen when a process (1) switches running -> waiting, (2) running -> ready, (3) waiting -> ready, (4) terminates. Scheduling under 1 and 4 is nonpreemptive; all others are preemptive.

question: Under nonpreemptive scheduling, once the CPU has been allocated to a process, the process keeps it until it:
options: Terminates or switches to the waiting state
Has run for one time quantum
Is preempted by a higher-priority process
hint: Nonpreemptive means the CPU is never taken away.
explanation: Slide 5.6: nonpreemptive scheduling happens only when the running process switches to waiting or terminates.

question: An I/O-bound program typically has:
options: A few very long CPU bursts
hint: It spends most of its time waiting for I/O.
explanation: Slide 5.4: process execution is a cycle of CPU execution and I/O wait. An I/O-bound program does little computing between I/O requests, so it has many short CPU bursts; a CPU-bound program has fewer, longer bursts.

question: A process is selected from the __________ queue by the __________ scheduler to be executed on the CPU.
hint: The selected process must already be ready.
explanation: Slide 5.6: the CPU scheduler selects from among the processes in the ready queue and allocates a CPU core to one of them.

question: Turnaround time is:
options: The total time from the arrival of a process until its completion
The time spent waiting in the ready queue only
The time until the first response is produced
The number of processes completed per time unit
hint: Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time.
explanation: Slides 5.8 and 5.49: turnaround time is the amount of time to execute a particular process: completion time - arrival time.

question: In priority scheduling, the CPU is allocated to the process with:
hint: In this course a smaller number means a more important process.
explanation: Slides 5.19 and 5.49: the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority; the smallest integer is the highest priority.

question: In which algorithm is the ready queue split into multiple queues, with processes classified into groups and unable to move between queues?
hint: Its 'feedback' version lets processes move.
explanation: Slides 5.22-5.24: the multilevel queue's ready queue consists of multiple queues (e.g. prioritized by process type). Only the multilevel feedback queue (slide 5.25) lets a process move between queues.

question: In which algorithm can a process move between the various queues?
hint: It defines methods to upgrade and demote processes.
explanation: Slide 5.25: in the multilevel feedback queue, a process can move between the various queues.

question: Response time is the amount of time from when a request is submitted until:
options: The first response is produced (not the output)
The process enters the ready queue
hint: It matters most for time-sharing environments.
explanation: Slide 5.8: response time - amount of time it takes from when a request was submitted until the first response is produced, not output (for time-sharing environments).

question: Maximum CPU utilization is obtained with:
hint: CPU scheduling is the basis of these operating systems.
explanation: Slide 5.4: maximum CPU utilization is obtained with multiprogramming.

question: In which algorithm does each process get a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum?
hint: After the quantum elapses the process goes to the end of the ready queue.
explanation: Slide 5.15: in RR each process gets a small unit of CPU time (time quantum q), usually 10-100 milliseconds.

question: Round Robin is basically a __________ scheduling algorithm designed for __________ systems.
hint: It gives each user a turn quickly.
explanation: Slide 5.15: RR preempts a process when its quantum expires; it typically gives better response (slide 5.16), which suits time-sharing.

question: Which of the following is NOT a CPU scheduling algorithm covered in the chapter?
hint: The covered ones are FCFS, SJF, SRTF, RR, priority and multilevel queues.
explanation: Slides 5.10-5.26 cover FCFS, SJF, SRTF, RR, priority (with and without RR), multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue.

question: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process an equal share of the CPU (1/n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q)?
hint: n processes and a quantum q.
explanation: Slide 5.15: with n processes and quantum q, each process gets 1/n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q time units at once.

question: The number of processes that complete their execution per time unit is called:
hint: It counts finished processes.
explanation: Slide 5.8: throughput - number of processes that complete their execution per time unit.

question: In preemptive priority scheduling, when a new process arrives at the ready queue, its priority is compared with the priority of the:
hint: Preemption can only take the CPU from one process.
explanation: Slide 5.19: priority scheduling can be preemptive; the newly arrived process takes the CPU if its priority is higher than the running process's priority.

question: A multiprocessor system has 4 processors, each with 3 cores (one hardware thread per core). What is the maximum number of instructions that can execute at the same time?
hint: Each core can execute independently.
explanation: Slide 5.33: each core on the chip can execute in parallel, so 4 processors x 3 cores = 12 instructions at a time.

question: Which CPU-scheduling algorithm usually has the highest context-switch overhead?
options: Round Robin with a small quantum
hint: The timer interrupts every quantum to schedule the next process.
explanation: Slides 5.15 and 5.17: RR switches every quantum; if q is small, the overhead becomes too high, so q must be large with respect to the context-switch time.

question: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P2, P3, P1 with CPU bursts P1 = 12 ms, P2 = 1.5 ms and P3 = 1.5 ms. What is the average waiting time under FCFS?
hint: Run them in the order they arrived; waiting time = start time here.

question: Five processes arrive together in the order P1..P5 with CPU bursts 9, 8, 7, 6 and 5 ms. Round Robin with q = 9 ms produces exactly the same schedule as which algorithm?
hint: Can any process be preempted when every burst is at most q?
explanation: Slide 5.15: if q is at least as large as every burst, no process is preempted and RR behaves like FIFO, running P1..P5 in arrival order. SJF and SRTF would run the shortest job (P5) first, so they differ.

question: Process execution consists of a cycle of:
hint: A CPU burst is followed by an I/O burst.
explanation: Slide 5.4: CPU-I/O burst cycle - process execution consists of a cycle of CPU execution and I/O wait; the CPU burst distribution is of main concern.

question: Which of the following scheduling decision points is preemptive?
options: A process switches from running to ready
A process switches from running to waiting
hint: In this case the process could still use the CPU.
explanation: Slide 5.6: scheduling under (1) running -> waiting and (4) termination is nonpreemptive; all other scheduling, including running -> ready, is preemptive.

question: Which issue must be considered when using preemptive scheduling?
options: The size of the bootstrap program
The number of hard disk sectors
hint: A process may be interrupted in the middle of updating something.
explanation: Slide 5.6: with preemptive scheduling, consider access to shared data, preemption while in kernel mode, and interrupts occurring during crucial OS activities.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the dispatcher's steps?
options: Selecting which process should run next
Jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart it
hint: The decision is made by another component before the dispatcher acts.
explanation: Slide 5.7: the dispatcher gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location. Selection is the CPU scheduler's job.

question: Waiting time, as a scheduling criterion, is the amount of time a process has spent:
options: From arrival to its first response
hint: It does not include time actually running.
explanation: Slide 5.8: waiting time - amount of time a process has been waiting in the ready queue.

question: What is the main difficulty of SJF scheduling?
options: Knowing the length of the next CPU request
It never gives the minimum average waiting time
It cannot be used with arriving processes
hint: The scheduler would need to predict the future.
explanation: Slides 5.12 and 5.14: the difficulty is knowing the length of the next CPU request; it can be asked from the user or estimated, similar to the previous bursts.

question: The preemptive version of SJF is called:
hint: It compares what is left of each burst.
explanation: Slide 5.14: the preemptive version of SJF is called shortest-remaining-time-first.

question: Round Robin is used with 5 processes in the ready queue and a time quantum of 20 ms. What is the maximum time any process waits before getting its next turn?
hint: Every other process may run one full quantum before it.
explanation: Slide 5.15: no process waits more than (n-1)q time units: (5-1) x 20 = 80 ms.

question: What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is too small?
hint: q must be large with respect to something.
explanation: Slide 5.15: q small - q must be large with respect to the context switch, otherwise the overhead is too high.

question: According to the slides, typical values are a time quantum of about __________ and a context switch of less than __________.
hint: The quantum is much larger than the switch time.
explanation: Slide 5.16: q usually 10 ms to 100 ms, context switch < 10 usec.

question: As a rule of thumb for choosing the time quantum in RR, what percentage of CPU bursts should be shorter than q?
hint: Most bursts should finish within one slice.
explanation: Slide 5.18: 80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than q.

question: Compared with SJF, Round Robin typically has:
options: Higher average turnaround time but better response
Lower average turnaround time and worse response
The same turnaround time and response
hint: RR is fair to all processes, which helps interactivity.
explanation: Slide 5.16: RR typically has higher average turnaround than SJF, but better response.

question: In Round Robin, how does the OS take the CPU back when a quantum ends?
options: A timer interrupt occurs every quantum
hint: The same hardware that prevents infinite loops.
explanation: Slide 5.15: timer interrupts every quantum to schedule the next process.

question: In priority scheduling combined with Round Robin:
options: The highest-priority process runs, and processes with the same priority run round-robin
All processes run round-robin regardless of priority
Priorities are ignored when a quantum expires
hint: RR is only used to break ties.
explanation: Slide 5.21: run the process with the highest priority; processes with the same priority run round-robin.

question: Which of the following is NOT a parameter that defines a (plain) multilevel queue scheduler?
options: The method used to decide when to upgrade a process
The scheduling algorithm for each queue
hint: Processes in this scheduler never change queues.
explanation: Slide 5.22: a multilevel queue is defined by the number of queues, the algorithm for each queue, the method to determine which queue a process enters, and scheduling among the queues. Upgrade/demote methods belong to the multilevel feedback queue (slide 5.25).

question: In a multilevel queue with priority scheduling, which queue is scheduled first?
options: The queue with the oldest process
hint: Each priority has its own queue.
explanation: Slide 5.23: with priority scheduling, have separate queues for each priority and schedule the process in the highest-priority queue.

question: Aging can be implemented using:
options: A multilevel queue with fixed assignment
hint: Old processes need a way to move up.
explanation: Slide 5.25: aging can be implemented using a multilevel feedback queue, since a process can be upgraded to a higher queue.

question: A multilevel feedback queue has Q0: RR with q = 8 ms, Q1: RR with q = 16 ms, and Q2: FCFS. A new process needs a single CPU burst of 30 ms and no other processes exist. How much of its burst runs in Q2?
hint: Follow the process down the queues.
explanation: Slide 5.26: a new process enters Q0 and receives 8 ms; if not finished it moves to Q1 and receives 16 more ms; then it moves to Q2. 30 - 8 - 16 = 6 ms run in Q2.

question: In the example multilevel feedback queue (Q0 RR 8 ms, Q1 RR 16 ms, Q2 FCFS), what happens to a process that does not finish within its 8 ms in Q0?
options: It is moved directly to Q2
hint: Processes move down one level at a time.
explanation: Slide 5.26: if it does not finish in 8 ms, the process is moved to Q1; if it still doesn't complete there, it is preempted and moved to Q2.

question: When the thread library schedules user-level threads to run on an LWP (in many-to-one and many-to-many models), this is known as:
hint: The competition happens within one process.
explanation: Slide 5.27: the thread library schedules user-level threads on an LWP; this is process-contention scope (PCS), since competition is within the process. Kernel threads scheduled onto a CPU use system-contention scope (SCS).

question: A kernel thread scheduled onto an available CPU competes with all threads in the system. This is called:
hint: The competition is system-wide.
explanation: Slide 5.27: a kernel thread scheduled onto an available CPU is system-contention scope (SCS) - competition among all threads in the system.

question: When an operating system supports threads, what does the scheduler schedule?
hint: The slide states this directly.
explanation: Slide 5.27: when threads are supported, threads are scheduled, not processes.

question: In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP):
options: One master processor schedules all others
Only one processor runs user code
hint: Threads may be in a common ready queue or private per-processor queues.
explanation: Slide 5.32: SMP is where each processor is self-scheduling; all threads may be in a common ready queue, or each processor may have its own private queue.

question: In a multithreaded multicore system, what does a core do when one hardware thread has a memory stall?
options: Stops all threads until the memory returns
Moves the thread to the wait queue on disk
hint: Each core has more than one hardware thread.
explanation: Slides 5.33-5.34: each core has more than one hardware thread; if one thread has a memory stall, the core switches to another thread to make progress while memory retrieval happens.

question: Windows uses which type of CPU scheduling?
hint: The highest-priority thread runs next.
explanation: Slide 5.42: Windows uses priority-based preemptive scheduling; the highest-priority thread runs next, and the dispatcher is the scheduler.

question: Which formula gives the waiting time of a process?
options: Waiting time = turnaround time - burst time
Waiting time = completion time - arrival time
Waiting time = burst time - arrival time
Waiting time = completion time + burst time
hint: Remove the time the process actually spent running.
explanation: Slide 5.49: turnaround time = completion time - arrival time; waiting time = turnaround time - burst time.

question: Which formula gives the turnaround time of a process?
hint: From the moment it arrives until the moment it finishes.
explanation: Slide 5.49: turnaround time = completion time - arrival time.

question: A CPU completes 5 processes in a total execution time of 40 ms. What is the throughput?
hint: Throughput = number of processes completed / total execution time.
explanation: Slide 5.49: throughput = number of processes completed / total execution time = 5 / 40 = 0.125 processes per ms (one process every 8 ms).

question: Burst time is defined as:
options: The time required by a process for CPU execution
The time at which the process arrives
The time at which the process completes
The time spent waiting in the ready queue
hint: It is how long the process needs the CPU.
explanation: Slide 5.49: burst time - time required by a process for CPU execution. Arrival time is when it arrives in the ready queue; completion time is when it completes.
